questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving types — typeof.

options.misconception: Assuming the literal is quoted text
Confusing a primitive with an object
Thinking the variable was never set

questions.explanation: typeof reports 'number' for numeric primitives such as 694. Arrays and objects also report 'object', but a plain integer reports 'number'. The printed value is number, while the alternatives come from assuming the literal is quoted text, confusing a primitive with an object and thinking the variable was never set.
questions.hint: typeof returns a lowercase type name string.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving types — number isnan.

options.misconception: Assuming dividing a number by text yields a number
Confusing the test with the value tested

questions.explanation: Dividing 695 by a non-numeric string produces NaN, and Number.isNaN returns true for that value. The global isNaN would first coerce, which differs from the strict method. The printed value is true, while the alternatives come from assuming dividing a number by text yields a number, confusing the test with the value tested and thinking the conversion throws.
questions.hint: Number.isNaN does not coerce its argument.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving types — parseint.

options.misconception: Taking the radix as the result

questions.explanation: parseInt reads leading digits in base ten and returns the number 696. The radix argument selects the base; it is not part of the answer. The printed value is 696, while the alternatives come from rounding the parsed value up, taking the radix as the result and applies a different mistaken operation.
questions.hint: The second argument names the numeric base.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving loops — for of.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 697.

questions.explanation: for...of iterates the element values, adding 697, 2 and 3 to reach 702. Unlike for...in, it does not visit property keys. The printed value is 702, while the alternatives come from counting only the first value, skipping the value two and reporting the loop count instead.
questions.hint: for...of yields values, not indexes.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving loops — for in.
questions.explanation: for...in visits the enumerable keys a and b, so the concatenated string has length two. The numeric values, including 698, are never visited by this loop. Carrying the operation through gives 2; common slips include assuming only one property is enumerable and counting the letter a twice.
questions.hint: for...in enumerates property names.

questions.subject: JAVASCRIPT
questions.learningObjective: Interpret JavaScript behavior demonstrated by a short executable snippet involving async — microtasks.

stimulus.body: A program is processing the value 699.

options.misconception: Running the callback before synchronous code

questions.explanation: Synchronous logs run first, then the promise callback drains in the microtask queue, producing start end 699. Microtasks wait until the current stack is empty. The printed value is start end 699, while the alternatives come from running the callback before synchronous code, reversing the synchronous logs and treating the promise as immediate.
questions.hint: Promise callbacks are microtasks, not synchronous calls.
